content.text: Mentorship and sustained practice develop skill and connect individuals to community and cultural heritage.
Through practice and mentorship, people turn skill into voice and work into art.
In Lesson 19, students finish reading Chapter 19 of
A Single Shard
, continue adding to their Stages of Learning graphic organizers, and discuss the roles of pride, foolishness, and motivation in the text.
This lesson supports discussion of apprenticeship and mentorship as well as making supporting claims.

Quick Write
Turn and Talk
Directions:
Take out the article “The Youngsters Keeping Traditional Trades Alive” and your homework from Lesson 17. Discuss the following with a partner:
Read “The Youngsters Keeping Traditional Trades Alive.”
Find two quotes from the text that show two different stages of learning.
Come up with one question about Tree-ear’s learning process so far, thinking about the stages he has been through and what he still must learn. Explain how this relates to the theme of mentorship.
What trades are discussed in the article? What skills or mindsets are needed for a trade apprenticeship? Use examples from the article to support your ideas.
Conversation Norms
Directions:
Work together to develop conversation norms for the text-based group discussion.
"Listen without interrupting.”
Support ideas with evidence.”
“Use language from the text.”
“Respond to ideas rather than individuals.”
Part A: Preparing for Discussion
Preparing for Fishbowl Conversation
Directions:
During the discussion today, you’re going to follow the
Fishbowl Conversation
routine. This routine helps us build meaning together instead of just sharing separate opinions. Here’s how it works:
The class will be split into two groups: one will sit in a circle in the middle of the room (the inner circle), and the other will sit in a circle around the first group (the outer circle).
Students in the inner circle will have 10 minutes to discuss the question prompts.

While the inner circle group is discussing, the outer circle group will silently take notes on the inner circle’s discussion to add to their own thinking and provide responses to points brought up by the inner circle.
After 10 minutes, the groups will switch places, and the new inner circle group will have their turn to discuss the question prompts while the new outer circle group silently takes notes.
Review the question prompts for the Fishbowl Conversation.
How does an apprentice navigate the stages of learning in order to succeed in a craft? Use textual evidence to support your ideas.
Across Chapters 1–8 of
A Single Shard

, what patterns show how observation, trying, and failing help Tree-ear grow as a learner? Which moments best demonstrate how difficult learning actually works? Use textual evidence to support your ideas.
What does it take to learn something difficult? Cite examples from the novel and the article to support your ideas.
Pulse Check
Which statement best summarizes what both texts suggest about learning a difficult task?
Learning a trade depends mostly on natural talent.
Apprentices must work independently, without guidance from others.
Learning something difficult requires observation, practice, and perseverance.
Young people prefer traditional trades because they are easier than other careers.
Part B: Fishbowl Conversation
Fishbowl Conversations
Directions:
Now we will engage in the
Fishbowl Conversation
routine using the agreed upon norms. Remember to refer to your Accountable Talk Sentence Stems to help you phrase your questions and comments. Also use your
Reflect-and-Respond
graphic organizer to record questions and ideas as they come up during the discussion.
Quick Write
Directions:
Write a one- to two-sentence response to the following prompt:
What is one new connection you made between the novel
A Single Shard
, the article “The Youngsters Keeping Traditional Trades Alive,” and the stages of learning?
Turn and Talk
Say These Directions:
Take out the article “The Youngsters Keeping Traditional Trades Alive” and your homework from Lesson 17.
Review the homework assignment:
Read “The Youngsters Keeping Traditional Trades Alive.”
Find two quotes from the text that show two different stages of learning.
Come up with one question about Tree-ear’s learning process so far, thinking about the stages he has been through and what he still must learn. Explain how this relates to the theme of mentorship.
Say:
Share with your partner the two quotes from the text that connect to the stages of learning. Also share your questions and discuss how they relate to the theme of mentorship.
Say These Directions:
Turn and Talk
to respond to the following questions.
Ask:
What trades are discussed in the article? What skills or mindsets are needed for a trade apprenticeship? Use examples from the article to support your ideas.

Some trades discussed are leatherworking, globe making, clog making, wheelwrighting, and papermaking. The skills and mindsets needed are “common sense, good eyesight, and to be good with their hands,” as well as interest in the craft, ambition, risk-taking, ability to work with tools, belief in learning and passing down ancient skills, and enjoyment/ability to work with your hands.
Invite two or three pairs to share their responses with the class.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Today, you will engage in a
Fishbowl Conversation
, a type of class discussion, using information from the article that you read for homework.
Students will review their homework responses from the previous lesson and engage in a Turn and Talk to discuss prompts about the article “The Youngsters Keeping Traditional Trades Alive.”
Conversation Norms

Lead students in a co-construction of the conversation norms they will be following during today’s group discussion. You may follow the sequence below, or, if time permits, allow students to identify and name norms using a less structured format.
Display each identified norm for students to see during discussion.
Say These Directions:
Work together to develop conversation norms for the text-based group discussion.
Say:
Our first norm will focus on listening.
Ask:
Why is it important to listen during a discussion?
An effective discussion has a balance between listening and speaking, giving everyone a chance to share their ideas and taking time to think about others’ points before responding.
Say:
We can call this norm "Listen without interrupting.” This means that group members take turns, one voice at a time, waiting until a speaker finishes before responding.
Say:
Our second norm will be about using evidence to support ideas.
Ask:
Why is it important to use evidence to support your ideas?
When discussing a text, you don’t just share ideas; you support them with details from a text or other source so that people know where your ideas came from.
Say:
This norm can be: “Support ideas with evidence.” When you provide evidence, include a page number or describe the excerpt so others can find it. This way, others can see where your ideas came from.
Say:
The next norm focuses on using language from the text to express our ideas.
Ask:
Why is it important to use language from the text?
Using specific language from the text to explain your ideas gives a speaker credibility and also keeps the discussion grounded in the text.
Say:

This norm can be: “Use language from the text.” This includes referencing specific names of people, places, and concepts in fiction, as well as using domain-specific or technical vocabulary in informational texts.
Say:
Our final norm should focus on how we respond: in a strong discussion we address ideas rather than individuals, using both a respectful tone and language.
Ask:
Why do you think it’s important to respond to ideas rather than individuals?

If you react to individuals, they might take it personally. Responding to ideas keeps the discussion on the text and people won’t feel as though they are being criticized if you disagree with their ideas.
Say:
Let’s write the norm, “Respond to ideas rather than individuals.” Instead of labeling a comment as “wrong,” we explain our thinking using evidence.
Teacher Tip
Encourage students to use their Unit Vocabulary graphic organizers or Personal Dictionaries to support domain-specific language use during the
Fishbowl Conversation
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Understanding conversation norms
Briefly model how a student might respond to a peer during the
Fishbowl Conversation

using a sentence frame and evidence. Ex. “I think ____. On p. __, the text shows ____.” Ex. “I agree with the idea that ____ because the text shows ____.” Ex. “Can you point to a line that supports that idea?”
Ready for extension: Adding on and challenging

Invite students to use the following sentence frames to challenge a point made by a peer using evidence during the discussion. Ex. “I agree with ____, and I want to challenge it by adding the point that ____. The text on page __ supports the idea that ____.” Ex. “Another way to think about ____ is ____. The writer’s ____ (word choice/use of dialogue/use of images) makes the reader think ____.”
Support students in co-constructing discussion norms that directly enable synthesis across texts (listen, cite, build, question), preparing them for accountable Fishbowl Conversations.
Invite students to use their home language privately to plan ideas, then present in English with stems (planning as a strength, not a barrier).
Convert each norm into an observable action (what it looks/sounds like).
Add one “evidence norm” and one “synthesis norm” explicitly (not just “be respectful”).
Post stems where students can see them during the Fishbowl Conversation.
Turn abstract norms into sentence stems (“I agree because . . . ,” “A detail from the article shows . . .”).
Add probing-question language (“Can you point to . . . ,” “What makes you say that?”).
Model one short “build” move linking two peers.
I agree with ___ because ___ (p. __ / in the article . . .).
I want to add on: across both texts, ___.
Can you clarify what evidence shows that?
A different way to interpret that is ___ because ___.
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become more independent.
Emerging:
"One example from the novel is ___." / "One example from the article is ___."
Expanding:
"In both texts, ___." / "According to the text, this shows ___."
Bridging:
"Across both texts, ___." / "Taken together, this suggests ___."
If norms stay generic (“be nice”) → Prompt: What exact words can you use to disagree respectfully?
If students forget evidence expectation → Prompt: Add “According to . . .” to your sentence.
Students can name at least 3 norms in action form.
Students can produce one evidence-based stem aloud.
Students can produce one probing question stem.

Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to support and expand student use of academic language, and provide scaffolding as needed.
Emerging:
Names one piece of evidence from each source using a frame.
Expanding:
Cites moments from both texts and explains what each shows.
Bridging:
Cites specific moments from both texts and builds a warrant connecting them.
Connection to Today’s Learning
Say:
Today, you will participate in a
Fishbowl Conversation
to discuss
A Single Shard
and the article “The Youngsters Keeping Traditional Trades Alive.” During the activity, use the agreed-upon conversation norms to help you listen and respond to your classmates.
Students will construct a list of conversation norms for their Fishbowl Conversation.
Part A: Preparing for Discussion (SL.6.1, SL.6.4) (10 minutes)
Preparing for Fishbowl Conversation

Provide students with Accountable Talk sentence stems and Reflect-and-Respond graphic organizers to support their participation in the discussion. Explain that the sentence stems can guide them in agreeing, disagreeing, and building on others’ ideas, while the Reflect-and-Respond graphic organizer can be used to record questions, ideas, and observations before, during, and after the discussion.
Before students prepare for their group discussion, explain the
Fishbowl Conversation
routine.
Say These Directions:
During the discussion today, you’re going to follow the
Fishbowl Conversation
routine. This routine helps us build meaning together instead of just sharing separate opinions. Here’s how it works:
The class will be split into two groups: one will sit in a circle in the middle of the room (the inner circle), and the other will sit in a circle around the first group (the outer circle).
Students in the inner circle will have 10 minutes to discuss the question prompts.

While the inner circle group is discussing, the outer circle group will silently take notes on the inner circle’s discussion to add to their own thinking and provide responses to points brought up by the inner circle.
After 10 minutes, the groups will switch places, and the new inner circle group will have their turn to discuss the question prompts while the new outer circle group silently takes notes.

Provide students with the question prompts they will be discussing during the Fishbowl Conversation. Then model a response to at least one of the question prompts using discussion stems and examples (see the sample responses below).
Ask:
How does an apprentice navigate the stages of learning in order to succeed in a craft? Use textual evidence to support your ideas.

An apprentice navigates the stages of learning by seeking out opportunities to observe and to try. For example, the article explains how leatherworking apprentice Leighann Perry became interested in her trade after observing leatherworking at a museum and then looked for a way to learn the skill.
Ask:
Across Chapters 1–8 of
A Single Shard

, what patterns show how observation, trying, and failing help Tree-ear grow as a learner? Which moments best demonstrate how difficult learning actually works? Use textual evidence to support your ideas.

Chapters 1–8 show how observing, trying, and failing are a part of a cycle. For example, Tree-ear observes other potters cutting clay from the riverbank. He tries to replicate their actions and instead gets his spade stuck. He tries again and eventually succeeds. Once he has learned this skill, he observes, tries, and fails at other parts of the pottery-making process, such as purifying the clay to the exact right consistency.
Ask:
What does it take to learn something difficult? Cite examples from the novel and the article to support your ideas..
Both the novel and the article show that learning something difficult takes perseverance and risk. In
A Single Shard

, Tree-ear takes risks by asking Min for an apprenticeship and continues to work hard even when he struggles or things don’t go his way. Min perseveres and takes risks when he tries, fails, and works to perfect the technique developed by Kang. In the article, the globe-making apprentice Eddy da Silva explains how he took a risk to pursue his interest: “The 24-year-old, who was born in Venezuela but now lives in England’s capital, left a corporate environment to pursue the craft but said ‘only a handful of people supported my decision.’”
Teacher Tip
Invite students to stop you and ask questions as you model the procedure. Highlight and discuss when/why/how you use citing/reporting verbs (
demonstrates
requires
shows
suggests
) and cause–and–effect language (
because
so that

) to support your points. Tell students that during their discussion, they should focus on grounding their ideas and responses in textual and visual evidence from both texts. Students can use the Accountable Talk Sentence Stems graphic organizer for examples of discussion stems they can use during the Fishbowl Conversation.
Preparing for Discussion
Instruct students to prepare for the Fishbowl Conversation by reviewing the prompts and preparing textual evidence from both texts to support their ideas.
Say:
Before we begin the
Fishbowl Conversation

, review your responses to the prompts and prepare textual evidence from both texts to support your ideas. Take a few minutes to review the novel and article to locate specific pieces of evidence you plan to use. Mark the page number or paragraph so you can clearly reference the evidence during the discussion.
Pulse Check (RI 6.1, RL 6.1)
Which statement best captures what both texts suggest about learning a challenging task?
Learning a trade depends mostly on natural talent.
Incorrect: The texts show that success comes from practice and perseverance, not natural talent alone.
Apprentices must work independently, without guidance from others.
Incorrect: Both texts emphasize mentorship and guidance, not learning alone.
Learning something difficult requires observation, practice, and perseverance.
Correct: Both texts show that learning requires observation, practice, and persistence.
Young people prefer traditional trades because they are easier than other careers.
Incorrect: The texts show that traditional trades are difficult and demanding, not easy.
Help students prepare Fishbowl Conversation contributions by organizing claims and evidence from both texts and rehearsing synthesis language before discussion begins.
Encourage students to use their own learning experiences as a quick “hook,” then pivot to textual proof (“That’s similar to Tree-ear when . . .”).
Have students annotate their notes with N (novel) and A (article) to ensure balance.
Prompt students to select “best evidence” (not the longest).
Convert summaries into claims (“This shows that learning requires . . .”).
Model synthesis phrasing: “Taken together, these sources suggest . . .”
Encourage precise verbs: shows, demonstrates, suggests, reveals.
My claim is ___. In
A Single Shard
(p. __), ___ shows ___. In the article, ___ shows ___. Taken together, this suggests ___.
One pattern across both texts is ___.
A key difference is ___, which matters because ___.
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become independent.
Emerging:
“In the novel, ___ shows ___.” / “In the article, ___ shows ___.”
Expanding:
“My claim is ___. According to A Single Shard (p. __), ___, and the article shows ___.”
Bridging:
“My claim is ___. In A Single Shard (p. __), ___ shows ___; in the article, ___ shows ___. Taken together, this suggests ___.”
Require a simple prep structure: claim → evidence (novel) → evidence (article) → synthesis sentence.
If students have evidence from only one text → Prompt: Add one supporting detail from the other text.
If students have facts only → Prompt: Add an interpretation sentence using “This suggests . . .”
Students prepare at least one claim supported by two sources.
Students use one synthesis phrase accurately.
Students include location language (page/section).
Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to scaffold up or release supports.
Emerging:
Prepares one claim with one piece of evidence from each text using a frame.
Expanding:
Prepares a claim supported by both texts and rehearses one synthesis phrase aloud.
Bridging:
Prepares a precise claim with cited evidence from both texts and uses location language plus a synthesis phrase.
Part B: Fishbowl Conversation (SL.6.1, SL.6.4) (20 minutes)
Fishbowl Conversation
Say These Directions:
Now we will engage in the
Fishbowl Conversation
routine using the agreed upon norms. Remember to refer to your
Accountable Talk Sentence Stems
to help you phrase your questions and comments. Also use your
Reflect-and-Respond
graphic organizer to record questions and ideas as they come up during the discussion.
Divide students into the inner circle and outer circle groups. After 10 minutes, have the groups switch places so that all students have the chance to contribute to the discussion.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with: Inner circle discussion

Give a simple two-step routine that keeps students focused on stating a claim and offering evidence from one or both texts. Step 1: State a claim. Ex. “I noticed that the article makes the point ____.” Ex. “I believe an important point is that ____.” Step 2: Prove the claim with details from the texts. Ex. “The article says ____, which shows ____.” Ex. “This connects to
A Single Shard
when ____ (p. __) because ____.” Remind students to face the inner circle, speak at a conversational volume, and pause briefly after their claim to ensure the outer circle can track the evidence.
Struggling with: Outer circle note-taking
Give a two-step routine that helps students capture what was said and what evidence supports it. Step 1: Track the conversation. Ex. “____ argued that ____, using the article ____ (section __)/
A Single Shard

(p. __).” Step 2: Prepare one response to share when circles switch. Organize your response so you first acknowledge the speaker’s point, then present your evidence in a sequence that builds on what they said. Ex. “I heard someone say ____, and I can add ____ from the article (section __)/
A Single Shard
Ready for extension: Making connections
Ask:
How are the depictions of the stages of learning in
A Single Shard

similar to and different from the way they are shown in the article “The Youngsters Keeping Traditional Trades Alive”? I noticed that both the novel and the article describe the experiences of young people learning a new skill and give insight into what they’re thinking and feeling during the process. For example, in
A Single Shard

, the author includes narration about Tree-ear observing, trying, failing, and refining, as well as details about his thoughts and feelings as he learns to make pottery. In the article, the writer gives firsthand accounts from apprentices about their experiences.
Support students in sustaining an evidence-based Fishbowl Conversation that synthesizes ideas across texts rather than producing disconnected comments.
Encourage students who speak less to enter with a prepared stem and one evidence card (short, planned contribution).
Inner circle: require each turn to include a claim and at least one cited detail.
Outer circle: require notes that capture claim and evidence and one follow-up question.
Midway switch: prompt new speakers to reference something previously said (“Building on . . .”).
Prompt synthesis moves: connect two speakers (“That relates to ___’s point because . . .”).
Upgrade vague agreement: “I agree, and the evidence that strengthens it is . . .”
Recast personal opinion into text-grounded reasoning.
Building on ___’s idea, the novel/article shows ___.
A detail that supports this is ___ (p. __ / article quote).
Taken together, these examples show ___.
Can you point to where the text suggests that?
Provide sentence frames for multilingual learners based on their proficiency levels as appropriate, and gradually reduce these supports as students become independent.
Emerging:
“The novel/article shows ___.” / “I agree with ___ because ___.”
Expanding:
“Building on ___’s idea, the novel/article shows ___ (p. __), which suggests ___.”
Bridging:
“Building on ___’s idea, A Single Shard shows ___ (p. __) and the article shows ___; taken together, these examples reveal ___.”
If students drift into personal stories only → Prompt: Connect back to a text moment.
If students quote without explanation → Prompt: Add “This shows . . .” and your claim.
Students reference both texts across the discussion (not just one).
Students ask at least one clarifying/probing question.
Students build on a peer’s idea with evidence.
Students at different proficiency levels may need to begin at different points within the task. Based on responses, look for opportunities to scaffold up or release supports.
Emerging:
Contributes one turn using a stem; cites one detail from a named text.
Expanding:
Builds on a peer’s idea with brief reasoning and cites a specific moment from at least one text.
Bridging:
Synthesizes peers’ ideas across both texts, cites specific moments with location language, and uses a synthesis phrase to draw a warrant.
Checklist
You will turn in your discussion notes for feedback. A strong draft should:
☐ Use accurate and relevant evidence from both texts, including where the evidence can be found.
☐ Explain the relationship between the stages of learning, how they help learners acquire difficult skills, and how they are represented in the texts.
☐ Explain relationships between events/ideas using domain-specific vocabulary and temporal connectors.
☐ Build on others’ ideas using Accountable Talk Sentence Stems while keeping comments relevant to the conversation and texts.
☐ Present claims and findings using appropriate eye contact, adequate volume, and clear pronunciation to ensure the audience can follow their reasoning.

Students will observe as the teacher explains the Fishbowl Conversation routine and models what students will be expected to do during the academic discussion. Students will then prepare for their Fishbowl Conversation by reviewing their homework responses.

Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English when indicated or appropriate.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information, and paraphrasing key ideas.

content.text: What does it take to learn something difficult?
